newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian students rock 'n roll for change.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian students rock 'n roll for change.

text.p: Sofia University reverberates with discordant sounds -- trumpets, whistles, harmonicas, cymbals, drums and tambourines -- the student protest band is warming up for another anti-government parade.
Each afternoon they assemble in the inner court of Sofia's ornate 19th Century university, often late but always ready to tweak the nose of the ruling Socialists.
"We call on those who built communism to destroy it," one banner proclaims.
Pots and kettles bang, shrill whistles blow, the motley army of students is on the move, led by a tractor draped with a banner saying: "Give me land and I'll give you bread".
For 28 days they have defied and mocked the Socialists -- the ex-Communist Party which ruled for 45 years until 1989 when it yielded to democracy and emerged as the Socialist Party.
On Sunday students blocked intersections leading to the airport. Sitting on tram lines they played backgammon, chess and cards while sporting badges which read: "The Game's Over."
The mood is festive with a street theatre theme each day: roping themselves together as "slaves", holding "Miss Protest" contests and burning worthless levs in front of money changers.

Caricatures are held aloft of Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov with a dangling Red Star earring and would-be prime minister Nikolai Dobrev with a Vodka bottle hung from his neck and a cigarette dangling from his lip.
"Communists can't jump!," shouts a student leader and everyone leaps up and down in delight, happy as well to be keeping warm in freezing temperatures.
Local residents wave from windows as 1,000 students march in noisy procession. Children hold up fingers in "Victory" signs while their parents wave and join in chants or songs.
To the tune of "When the Saints Go Marching In", students belt out a song which goes: "I don't want to be down under when the Socialists go falling down".
They stop at ministries to boo and chant "Mafia, Mafia". Passing elderly ladies, dolled up in tattered furs against the Balkan cold, smile and make "V" signs.

The students appear in an array of home-made costumes, from colourful top hats and Trojan helmets to a woman medical student wearing a surgical mask which says: "Be careful, the atmosphere is poisoned with communism".
The ragtag army is led by a sea of Bulgarian flags, many tied to long fishing poles or upside down to symbolise a nation in distress.
The students are united in the belief that the politicians should quit bickering and try to salvage the shattered economy.
"We are protesting against the hyperinflation, against the mess made by the Socialist Party," said Vladimir Harizanov, a student organiser.
"It's not political. It's economic. We're hungry. We eat only bread. We study without heat. If we're lucky, we live with our parents," he said.
The central student demand was that all parties join to stop the freefall of the lev and to check soaring inflation, now 50 percent a month, and then hold general elections.
Studying to be a school teacher, Harizanov said: "Everyone asks if we aren't tired after a month of protests. No, we aren't tired or afraid. We know it's now or never for change."
